newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, US aim to solve insurance row at next talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan, US aim to solve insurance row at next talks.

text.p: Japan and the United States aim to resolve their dispute on the Japanese insurance market at bilateral ministerial talks due to be held on December 6 and 7 in Tokyo, a senior Ministry of Finance official said on Tuesday.

The official said Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, and Ira Shapiro, senior negotiator at the U.S. Trade Representative's Office, may meet again before December 6 to lay groundwork for ministerial talks between Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and USTR Charlene Barshefsky.
Sakakibara and Shapiro met on Monday and Tuesday in Tokyo.

Summarising the two-day meeting, the ministry official said Japan and the United States remain still far apart on how to open Japan's $382 billion insurance market. "No major change occurred during the meeting," the official said.
"It is very difficult to say that we can reach an agreement at the ministerial meeting, but we will make utmost efforts to resolve the issue," the official said.

The official said there is almost no possibility of Mitsuzuka and Barshefsky meeting again before the December 15 deadline after their December 6-7 meeting. Japan and the U.S. have agreed to solve the dispute by the self-imposed deadline.
"Considering the parliamentary schedule in Japan, and Barshesfsky's schedule, the next meeting is the only opportunity for them to meet before the deadline," the official said.
"We have told U.S. negotiators that Japan is ready to make a compromise to resolve the insurance dispute, but we don't know if the U.S. side is ready to do so," the official said.

On Sunday, President Bill Clinton told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in a meeting on the sidelines of the summit of Asia-Pacific leaders in Manila that the row over deregulation of Japan's insurance market was their most important two-way trade problem.
Japan and the United States are at odds over implementation of a 1994 bilateral agreement to open Japan's $382 billion insurance market.

Washington had accused Tokyo of reneging on the agreement by moving to deregulate its "third sector" niche insurance market -- for such cover as personal accident and health care insurance -- in which foreign firms have a strong foothold, before opening its primary life and casualty markets.
The two nations originally set a July 31 deadline to settle the dispute, but agreed in October to push back the deadline to December 15.
